source_span: We now expect the FOMC to deliver a second 25bp hike in October, a change from our previous expectation that September would be the only hike.
source_chain: The FOMC hiked 25bp to 3.75-4% but was more hawkish than Goldman expected (16-2 for another hike, no dissents, median neutral rate up to 3.25%, Warsh's 'removed a dose of accommodation'), therefore Goldman abandoned its September-only call and now expects a second hike in October because consecutive-meeting hikes better fit the Fed's stated aim of a timelier return to 2% than an every-other-meeting pace, therefore market odds for October/December pricing rose while Goldman's terminal-rate forecast stayed unchanged; invalidation: additional hikes beyond October are not Goldman's base case because Goldman's own core PCE forecast (3.2%) sits below the FOMC's (3.4%), so its October call rests on the Fed's stated urgency rather than data Goldman itself expects to arrive.
pulse_chain: The hawkish dot plot and Warsh's rhetoric, not the hike itself, drove the market reaction (yields and bank/energy shares moving), therefore Goldman reversed its September-only call and added an October hike on the logic that back-to-back hikes serve the Committee's stated aim of a faster return to 2% versus skipping a meeting, while JPMorgan holds December per the median dot and reads the revisions as the Committee pivoting from supply-shock to demand-led overheating concern; invalidation: prints before the October 28 meeting decide whether the 51% priced probability is right, since Goldman's own 3.2% core PCE forecast trails the FOMC's 3.4%, meaning the October call is built on the Fed's stated urgency rather than the data Goldman expects.
why: The pulse reproduces Goldman's mechanism (dots over the hike drove the reversal to a consecutive-meeting October hike) and its invalidation (own sub-consensus core PCE forecast) intact and correctly attributed, alongside JPMorgan's distinct demand-led-overheating read at December.
